source_text: Anno quintodecimo principatus Tiberii proponit eum descendisse in ciuitatem Galilaeae Capharnaum, utique de caelo creatoris, in quod de suo ante descenderat. ecquid ergo ordinis fuerat, ut prius de suo caelo in creatoris descendens describeretur? cur enim non et ista reprehendam, quae non implent fidem ordinariae narrationis, deficientis in mendacio semper? plane semel dicta sint per quae iam alibi retractauimus: an descendens per creatorem, et quidem aduersus ipsum, potuerit ab eo admitti et inde tramitti in terram aeque ipsius. nunc autem et reliquum ordinem descensionis expostulo, tenens (descendisse) illum. uiderit enim, sicubi 'apparuisse* positum est. apparere subitum ex inopinato sapit conspectum, qui semel impegerit oculos in id, quod sine mora apparuit, descendisse autem dum fit uidetur et subicit oculos de facto. etiam ordinem facit atque ita cogit exigere, quali habitu, quali suggestu, quonam impetu uel temperamento, etiam quo in tempore diei noctisue descenderit; praeterea, quis uiderit descendentem, quis retulerit, quis adseuerauerit rem, utique nec adseueranti facile credendam. indignum denique, ut Romulus quidem ascensus sui in caelum habuerit Proculum adfirmatorem, Christus uero dei descensus de caelo sui non inuenerit adnuntiatorem, *** quasi non sic et ille ascenderit isdem mendacii scalis, sicut et iste descendit. quid autem illi cum Galilaea. si non erat creatoris, cui ista regio destinabatur ingressuro praedicationem, dicente Esaia: hoc primum bibito, cito facito, regio Zabulon et terra Nepthalim, et ceteri quimaritimam, etIordanis, Galilaea nationum. populus, qui sedetis in tenebris, uidete lumen magnum; qui habitatis terram, sedentes in umbra mortis, lumen ortum est super uos? bene autem, quod et deus Marcionis inluminator uindicatur nationum, quo magis debuerit, uel de caelo etsi descenderet, utique in Pontum potius descendere quam in Galilaeam. ceterum et loco et inluminationis opere secundum praedicationem occurrentibus Christo iam eum prophetatum incipimus agnoscere, ostendentem in primo ingressu uenisse se, non ut legem et prophetas dissolueret, sed ut potius adimpleret. hoc enim Marcion ut additum erasit. sed frustra negabit Christum dixisse quod statim fecit ex parte. prophetiam enim interim de loco adimpleuit: de caelo statim. ad synagogam. ut dici solet: 'ad quod uenimus, hoc age Marcion: aufer etiam illud de euangelio: non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israhel, et: non est auferre panem filiis et dare eum canibus, ne scilicet Christus Israhelis uideatur. sufficiunt mihi facta pro dictis. detrahe uoces Christi mei: res loquentur. ecce uenit in synagogam: certe ad oues perditas domus Israhelis. ecce doctrinae suae panem prioribus offert Israhelitis: certe, ut filios praefert. ecce aliis eum nondum impertit: certe, ut canes praeterit. quibus autem magis impertisset quam extraneis creatoris, si ipse inprimis non fuisset creatoris? et tamen quomodo in synagogam potuit admitti tam repentinus, tam ignotus, cuius nemo adhuc certus de tribu, de populo, de domo, de censu denique Augusti, quem testem fidelissimum dominicae natiuitatis Romana archiua custodiunt? Meminerant certe, nisi circumcisum scirent, non admittendum in sancta sanctorum. sed etsi passim synagoga adiretur, non tamen ad docendum nisi ab optime cognito et explorato et probato iam pridem in hoc ipsum uel aliunde commendato cum hoc munere. stupebant autem omnes ad doctrinam eius. plane. quoniam, inquit, in potestate erat sermo eius, non quoniam aduersus legem et prophetas docebat. utique enim eloquium diuinum et uim et gratiam praestabat, magis exstruens quam destruens substantiam legis et prophetarum. alioquin non stuperent, sed horrerent, nec mirarentur, sed statim auersarentur destructorem legis et prophetarum, et utique inprimis alterius dei praedi. catorem, quia nec potuisset aduersus legem et prophetas docere et hoc nomine aduersus creatorem non praemissa diuersae atque aemulae diuinitatis professione. cum ergo nihil tale scriptura significet, nisi solam uim et potestatem sermonis admirationi fuisse, facilius ostendit secundum creatorem docuisse illum, quia non negauit, quam aduersus creatorem, quia non significauit. atque ita aut eius erit agnoscendus, secundum quem docuit, aut praeuaricator iudicandus, si secundum eum, aduersus quem uenerat, docuit. exclamat ibidem spiritus daemonis: quid nobis et tibi est, Iesu uenisti perdere nos; scio qui sis, sanctus dei. hic ego non retractabo, an et hoc cognomentum competierit ei, quem nec Christum uocari oporteret, si non creatoris, — alibi iam de nominibus expostulatum est — at nunc discepto, quomodo hoc eum uocari cognouerit daemon, nulla umquam retro emissa praedicatione in illum a deo ignoto et in id temporis muto, cuius nec sanctum eum contestari potuit, ut ignoti (et)iam ipsi suo creatori. quid autem iam tale ediderat nouae diuinitatis. per quod posset alterius dei sanctus intellegi? tantum quod synagogam introgressus et nec sermone operatus (erat) aliquid aduersus creatorem? sicut ergo quem ignorabat nullo modo poterat Iesum et sanctum dei agnoscere, ita quem norat agnouit. nam et prophetam meminerat sanctum dei praedicasse et Iesum nomen domini esse in filio Naue. haec et ab angelo exceperat secundum nostrum euangelium: propterea quod in te nascetur uocabitur sanctum, filius dei, et uocabis nomen eius Iesum. sed et habebat utique sensum aliquem dominicae dispositionis — licet daemon tamen — magis quam alienae et nondum satis cognitae. nam et praemisit: quid nobis et tibi, Iesu? non quasi in extraneum, (sed) ad quem pertinent spiritus creatoris. nec enim dixit: 'quid tibi et nobis'? sed 'quid nobis et tibi'? se deplorans et sorti suae exprobrans. quam iam uidens adicit: uenisti perdere nos. adeo iudicis et ultoris et, ut ita dixerim, saeui dei filium agnouerat Iesum, non optimi illius, et perdere et punire nescientis. quorsum hunc locum praemisimus? ut Iesum et a daemone non alium doceamus agnitum et a semetipso non alium confirmatum quam creatoris. 'atquin', inquis, 'increpuit illum Iesus). plane, ut inuidiosum et in ipsa confessione petulantem, ut male adulantem, quasi haec esset summa gloria Christi, si ad perditionem daemonum uenisset et non potius ad hominum salutem, qui nec discipulos de subactione spirituum, sed de candida salutis gloriari uolebat. aut cur eum increpuit? si quasi mentitum in totum, ergo non fuit Iesus nec dei sanctus omnino; si quasi ex parte mentitum, quod eum legum quidem et sanctum dei, sed creatoris, existimasset, iniustissime increpuit hoc sentientem, quod sciebat sentiendum, et hoc non aestimantem, quod ignorabat aestimandum: alium legum et alterius dei sanctum. quodsi uerisimiliorem statum non habet increpatio nisi quem nos interpretamur, iam ergo et daemon nihil mentitus est, non ob mendacium increpitus; ipse enim erat Iesus, praeter quem alium daemon agnouisse non poterat, et Iesus eum confirmauit, quem agnouerat daemon, dum non ob mendacium increpat daemonem.
pass_a_gloss: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius, he proposes that he descended into the city of Galilee, Capharnaum, certainly from the heaven of the creator, into which he had previously descended from his own. What order was there, then, that he should first be described as descending from his own heaven into the creator's? Why should I not also reprehend these things, which do not fulfill the faith of the ordinary narrative, always failing in falsehood? Let what was once said be said again, which we have already retracted elsewhere: whether, descending through the creator, and indeed against him, he could have been admitted by him and sent from there into the earth, equally his own. Now, however, I demand the rest of the order of the descent, holding that he descended. For he sees, indeed, where it is written that he appeared. To appear suddenly, from the unexpected, has the flavor of a sudden sight, which, once it has struck the eyes on what appeared without delay, seems to have descended, and subjects the eyes to the fact. And it also makes an order and thus compels one to demand what kind of habit, what kind of suggestion, with what impetus or temperament, and also at what time of day or night he descended; furthermore, who saw him descending, who reported it, who confirmed the thing, which is not easily to be believed even by one who confirms it. It is finally unworthy that Romulus, indeed, had Proculus as a witness to his ascension into heaven, but Christ did not find an announcer of his descent from heaven, as if he did not also ascend by the same ladders of falsehood. What, then, does Galilee have to do with him? If it was not the creator's, to whom this region was destined for the entrance of preaching, saying, as Isaiah says: 'This first, drink quickly, region of Zabulon and land of Nepthalim, and the others by the sea, and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. A people who sit in darkness, see a great light; who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you?' But, indeed, it is well that the god of Marcion is also vindicated as the illuminator of the nations, so that he ought to have descended, even from heaven, rather into Pontus than into Galilee. Moreover, both in the place and in the work of illumination, according to the preaching that occurs to Christ, we begin to recognize him as already prophesied, showing in his first entrance that he came not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them. For Marcion has erased this as an addition. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what he immediately did in part. For he fulfilled the prophecy meanwhile, concerning the place, immediately, to the synagogue, as it is said: 'To what we have come, this we do.' Marcion, take away also that from the gospel: 'I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and: 'It is not to take the bread of the sons and give it to the dogs,' lest Christ seem to be of Israel. His deeds are enough for me in place of his words. Take away the voices of my Christ: the things speak. Behold, he comes into the synagogue: certainly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Behold, he offers the bread of his doctrine first to the Israelites: certainly, as he prefers the sons. Behold, he does not impart it to others: certainly, as he passes over the dogs. To whom would he have imparted it more than to the strangers of the creator, if he himself were not first of the creator? And yet, how could he have been admitted into the synagogue, so sudden, so unknown, whose no one was yet certain about the tribe, the people, the house, finally the census of Augustus, which the Roman archives keep as a most faithful witness of the Lord's birth? They certainly remembered, unless they knew he was circumcised, he was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue was entered in a disorderly manner, one was not admitted to teaching unless he was well known and explored and proven long before, either in this or in some other commendation. They were all amazed at his doctrine. Certainly, because his word was in power, not because he was teaching against the law and the prophets. For divine eloquence, indeed, presents both power and grace, rather building up than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise, they would not have been amazed, but would have been horrified, and would not have marveled, but would have immediately turned away from the destroyer of the law and the prophets, and especially from the preacher of another god, because he could not have taught against the law and the prophets without previously professing a different and rival divinity. Since, therefore, the scripture does not signify anything of this kind, but only the power and authority of the word to admiration, it more easily shows that he taught according to the creator, because it does not deny it, than against the creator, because it does not signify it. And so, either he is to be recognized as belonging to the one according to whom he taught, or he is to be judged as a transgressor, if he taught according to the one against whom he came. The spirit of the demon cries out there: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus? You have come to destroy us; I know who you are, the holy one of God.' I will not retract here whether this title also suited him, whom it was not fitting to call Christ, if not of the creator, — this has already been demanded elsewhere concerning the names — but now, as to the dispute, how the demon recognized him as being called this, with no preceding preaching about him from the unknown god, and at that time, when he could not even have testified that he was holy, as unknown even to his own creator. What, then, had he already brought forth of the new divinity, by which he could have been understood as the holy one of another god? Only that, having entered the synagogue, he had not yet worked anything with his word against the creator? Just as, therefore, the one whom he did not know could not in any way recognize Jesus as the holy one of God, so the one whom he knew recognized him. For he also remembered that the prophet had preached the holy one of God, and that Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. He had also received this from the angel, according to our gospel: 'Therefore, because he will be born in you, he will be called holy, the son of God, and you will call his name Jesus.' But he also had some sense of the Lord's disposition — although he was a demon — rather than of an alien and not yet sufficiently known one. For he also said beforehand: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus?' not as if to a stranger, but to one to whom the spirits of the creator pertain. For he did not say: 'What is there between you and us?' but 'What is there between us and you?' lamenting himself and reproaching his own fate. Which, seeing, he adds: 'You have come to destroy us.' So much did he recognize Jesus as the son of the judge and avenger, and, so to speak, of the severe God, not of the good one, who does not know how to destroy and punish. Why did we premise this passage? So that we may teach that Jesus was recognized by the demon, and not by another, and confirmed by himself, and not by another, as the one of the creator. 'But,' you say, 'Jesus rebuked him.' Certainly, as one who was envious and impudent, even in his confession, as one who was flattering badly, as if this were the greatest glory of Christ, if he had come to the destruction of the demons, and not rather to the salvation of men, who did not want his disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the pure glory of salvation. Or why did he rebuke him? If as one who had lied entirely, then Jesus was not the holy one of God at all; if as one who had lied in part, because he thought him to be the holy one of God, indeed, but of the creator, he rebuked him most unjustly, feeling what he knew was to be felt, and not estimating what he did not know was to be estimated: another holy one of the laws and of another god. But if the rebuke does not have a more probable status than what we interpret, then the demon lied about nothing, not rebuked because of falsehood; for he was Jesus, apart from whom the demon could not have recognized another, and Jesus confirmed what the demon had recognized, while not rebuking the demon because of falsehood.

pass_b_english: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius' reign, the story goes that Jesus descended into the city of Galilee, Capharnaum, from the creator's heaven, which he had previously entered from his own realm. But what's the logic behind this sequence of events? Why would Jesus first be described as descending from his own heaven into the creator's? It's worth questioning the narrative's consistency, especially since it often falls short of the truth. We've discussed this before, but let's revisit the idea: can Jesus, who supposedly descended through the creator and against him, really be admitted by the creator and sent to earth, which is also the creator's domain? Now, I'm demanding a clearer explanation of Jesus' descent, assuming it happened. The fact that he appeared suddenly, without warning, raises questions about the nature of his arrival. Did he just show up, or did he actually descend from heaven? The text says he appeared, but that doesn't necessarily mean he descended. We need to know more about the circumstances of his arrival, like what he was wearing, what his attitude was, and what time of day or night it was. Who witnessed his descent, and who reported it? These are crucial details that are lacking in the story. It's surprising that Romulus, a pagan figure, had a witness to his ascension into heaven, but Jesus, supposedly the son of God, didn't have anyone to announce his descent from heaven. This discrepancy suggests that Jesus' story might be fabricated, just like Romulus'. So, what's the connection between Jesus and Galilee? If Galilee wasn't part of the creator's territory, why did Jesus go there to preach? The prophet Isaiah had already spoken about this region, saying, 'This first, drink quickly, region of Zabulon and land of Nepthalim, and the others by the sea, and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. A people who sit in darkness, see a great light; who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you' (Isaiah 9:1-2). It's ironic that Marcion's god, who is supposed to be the illuminator of the nations, would choose to descend into Galilee rather than Pontus. As we examine Jesus' actions, we see that he fulfilled the prophecy by going to the synagogue and teaching. He didn't come to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfill them. Marcion, however, has erased this part of the story. Jesus' actions speak louder than his words. He went to the synagogue, which was a place for the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24). He offered his teachings to the Israelites first, showing that he preferred them over others. He didn't impart his teachings to everyone, which suggests that he was selective about who he taught. If Jesus wasn't part of the creator's plan, why did he focus on the Israelites? How could he have been admitted into the synagogue, given that he was a stranger with no known tribe, people, or family? The Roman archives, which kept records of the census, would have been aware of Jesus' background. The fact that he was circumcised would have been a requirement for him to be admitted into the holy of holies. Even if the synagogue was open to everyone, teaching was only allowed for those who were well-known and respected. The people were amazed at Jesus' doctrine, not because he was teaching against the law and the prophets, but because his words were powerful and authoritative. The demon in the synagogue recognized Jesus, saying, 'What is there between us and you, Jesus? You have come to destroy us; I know who you are, the holy one of God.' This recognition is significant, as it shows that the demon knew Jesus was the son of the creator, not some other god. The demon's words, 'What is there between us and you, Jesus?' suggest that he saw Jesus as a threat, someone who was going to destroy him. Jesus rebuked the demon, but not because the demon was lying. Instead, Jesus was correcting the demon's attitude, which was one of envy and flattery. The demon's recognition of Jesus as the holy one of God is a crucial point, as it shows that Jesus was indeed part of the creator's plan. The fact that Jesus confirmed the demon's recognition, rather than rebuking him for lying, suggests that the demon was telling the truth. This passage teaches us that Jesus was recognized by the demon, and not by another, as the one who belonged to the creator.

review.notes: Pass B fails on completeness and accuracy regarding the Latin text. 1. Pass B omits the specific argument regarding the 'order of descent' (the distinction between 'appearing' [apparuisse] and 'descending' [descendere]) which is a central logical pillar of the paragraph. 2. Pass B omits the detailed discussion of the demon's specific phrasing ('quid nobis et tibi' vs 'quid tibi et nobis') which Tertullian uses to argue the demon recognized the creator's spirit. 3. Pass B omits the concluding complex syllogism regarding whether the demon lied or not (the distinction between 'mentitum in totum' and 'ex parte mentitum'). 4. Pass B includes a summary/paraphrase style ('the story goes that', 'it's worth questioning', 'we've discussed this before') rather than a translation of the provided text. 5. Pass B fails to translate the specific details of the 'census of Augustus' and the 'Roman archives' as part of the argument for Jesus's known identity. 6. Pass B omits the specific mention of the 'son of Nun' (Naue) in relation to the name Jesus.
reasons: Pass B is a summary/paraphrase rather than a translation, omitting significant portions of the logical argumentation (the 'apparere' vs 'descendere' distinction, the specific word order of the demon's question, and the final complex conditional argument about the demon's lie).

reasons: Pass A fails to preserve the full sense of the Latin in multiple instances, such as 'apparuisse' being translated as 'appeared' but the Latin implies a more specific meaning of 'appeared' in the context of sudden appearance. 'sanctum dei' is accurately translated as 'holy one of God' in both Pass A and Pass B, but the full nuance of the Latin is not captured. 'daemon' is correctly translated as 'demon' in both versions, but the specific context of the demon's recognition of Jesus is not fully conveyed. 'Iesu' is correctly translated as 'Jesus' in both versions, but the full context of the demon's statement is not preserved. 'uenisti' is correctly translated as 'you have come' in both versions, but the nuance of the Latin is not fully captured.
